---
title: "A logistic regression analysis"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

We now carry the SuperTelicity analysis with one predictor from raw counts to fitted probabilities. The scientific question is descriptive: how does *in* completion use differ between manner and result verbs in this sample?

Recall that [maximum likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd) fixes the observed choices and asks which coefficient values assign them the greatest probability. Multiplying the row contributions uses an [independence](../foundations/independence.qmd) assumption. Repeated participants do not satisfy that assumption, so this simple fit gives us a benchmark for the later mixed model.

We proceed from the observed group counts to the fitted log odds contrast, its uncertainty, response scale predictions, and a check of what the row independent model leaves unresolved.

Recall that each [SuperTelicity response](why-generalized-linear-models.qmd) is one participant's *in* or *for* choice for one item. Here the analysis sequence is: (i) inspect cell counts, (ii) state and fit the Bernoulli logit model, (iii) interpret a response scale contrast, (iv) quantify uncertainty, and (v) check the fit's scope.

```{r}
#| label: logistic-application-data
#| echo: true
st <- read.csv("data/supertelicity/supertelicity-cloze.csv")
st$verb_type <- factor(st$verb_type, levels = c("manner", "result"))
raw_counts <- as.data.frame(table(st$verb_type, st$preposition))
names(raw_counts) <- c("verb_type", "preposition", "observations")
raw_counts
```

```{r}
#| label: logistic-application-fit
#| echo: true
fit <- glm(prep_in ~ verb_type, family = binomial(), data = st)
groups <- aggregate(prep_in ~ verb_type, st, mean)
groups$n <- as.integer(table(st$verb_type))
link_prediction <- predict(fit, newdata = groups, se.fit = TRUE)
groups$fitted <- plogis(link_prediction$fit)
groups$lower <- plogis(link_prediction$fit - qnorm(.975) * link_prediction$se.fit)
groups$upper <- plogis(link_prediction$fit + qnorm(.975) * link_prediction$se.fit)
groups
```

The output above also includes an interval for each fitted group probability. We first construct it on the log odds scale, where the regression calculation is approximately linear. A [**Wald interval**](https://online.stat.psu.edu/stat504/Lesson02) takes an estimate and adds or subtracts a reference multiplier times its standard error. Recall that the [standard error](../statistical-inference/standard-errors.qmd) is the estimated standard deviation of an estimator across repeated samples. For a 95% interval, the normal reference multiplier is $z_{.975}\approx1.96$. Thus the interval on the log odds scale is

$$
\widehat\eta_g\ \pm\ z_{.975}\operatorname{se}(\widehat\eta_g).
$$

Applying the inverse logit to each endpoint keeps the probability interval inside $(0,1)$. Because the inverse logit is nonlinear, equal distances around $\widehat\eta_g$ generally become unequal distances around $\widehat\pi_g$.

The fit reproduces the higher sample probability for result verbs, and the plot places that raw contrast beside the GLM intervals computed under row independence. On the link scale, the likelihood is

$$
\ell(\boldsymbol\beta)=\sum_i\left[y_i\eta_i-
\log(1+e^{\eta_i})\right],
\qquad \eta_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{result}_i.
$$

The [logistic score and Hessian](iteratively-reweighted-least-squares.qmd)
give the large sample coefficient covariance estimate

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}
(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
=
(\mathbf X^\top\widehat{\mathbf W}\mathbf X)^{-1},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathbf W}
=
\operatorname{diag}
\{\widehat\pi_i(1-\widehat\pi_i)\}.
$$

For a group design row $\mathbf x_g$, the fitted log odds are
$\widehat\eta_g=\mathbf x_g^\top\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ and their estimated
variance is

$$
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat\eta_g)
=
\mathbf x_g^\top
\widehat{\operatorname{Var}}(\widehat{\boldsymbol\beta})
\mathbf x_g.
$$

```{r}
#| label: logistic-application-information-check
X <- model.matrix(fit)
pi_hat <- fitted(fit)
coefficient_covariance_by_hand <- solve(crossprod(
  X,
  X * as.numeric(pi_hat * (1 - pi_hat))
))
coefficient_covariance_from_glm <- vcov(fit)

group_design <- model.matrix(~ verb_type, data = groups)
group_link_se_by_hand <- sqrt(diag(
  group_design %*%
    coefficient_covariance_by_hand %*%
    t(group_design)
))

stopifnot(
  max(abs(
    coefficient_covariance_by_hand - coefficient_covariance_from_glm
  )) < 1e-8,
  max(abs(group_link_se_by_hand - link_prediction$se.fit)) < 1e-7
)

data.frame(
  verb_type = groups$verb_type,
  direct_link_standard_error = group_link_se_by_hand,
  predict_link_standard_error = link_prediction$se.fit
)
```

The inverse Hessian treats the fitted likelihood curvature as an approximation
to sampling variation in the coefficients. The direct matrix calculation
reproduces both `vcov()` and the standard errors returned by `predict()`.

```{r}
#| label: logistic-application-plot
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(groups, aes(verb_type, prep_in)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), color = "#1F5A85") +
  geom_point(size = 2.3) +
  labs(x = "Verb type", y = "Probability of an in-completion") +
  theme_classic()
```

Maximizing it yields the coefficient estimates printed below.

```{r}
#| label: logistic-application-coefficients
#| echo: true
summary(fit)$coefficients
```

The substantive target is the fitted result-minus-manner probability contrast:

```{r}
#| label: logistic-application-response-contrast
#| echo: true
with(groups, c(result_minus_manner = fitted[verb_type == "result"] -
                                      fitted[verb_type == "manner"]))
```

For a likelihood based comparison, `confint()` uses a **profile likelihood**. To profile one coefficient, we hold it at a sequence of candidate values and maximize over the remaining coefficients at each candidate. The resulting likelihood curve tells us which candidate values remain sufficiently compatible with the observed data, without requiring the curve to be exactly quadratic near the estimate. The endpoints below remain on the coefficient's log odds scale until transformed.

For a candidate result-verb coefficient $b_1$, write

$$
\ell_{\mathrm{profile}}(b_1)
=
\max_{b_0}\ell(b_0,b_1).
$$

A 95% profile likelihood interval retains candidate values satisfying

$$
2\left[
\ell(\widehat\beta_0,\widehat\beta_1)
-\ell_{\mathrm{profile}}(b_1)
\right]
\leq
\chi^2_{1,.95}.
$$

The endpoints occur where the two sides are equal. We solve those equations
directly from the observed SuperTelicity choices.

```{r}
#| label: logistic-profile-interval
#| echo: true
bernoulli_log_likelihood <- function(intercept, slope, y, result) {
  eta <- intercept + slope * result
  log_normalizer <- pmax(eta, 0) + log1p(exp(-abs(eta)))
  sum(y * eta - log_normalizer)
}

profile_log_likelihood <- function(slope) {
  intercept_search <- optimize(
    function(intercept) -bernoulli_log_likelihood(
      intercept,
      slope,
      y = st$prep_in,
      result = as.numeric(st$verb_type == "result")
    ),
    interval = c(-20, 20),
    tol = 1e-12
  )
  -intercept_search$objective
}

maximum_log_likelihood <- as.numeric(logLik(fit))
cutoff <- qchisq(0.95, df = 1)
profile_equation <- function(slope) {
  2 * (maximum_log_likelihood - profile_log_likelihood(slope)) - cutoff
}
slope_estimate <- coef(fit)[["verb_typeresult"]]
slope_se <- coef(summary(fit))["verb_typeresult", "Std. Error"]
direct_profile_link <- c(
  lower = uniroot(
    profile_equation,
    c(slope_estimate - 10 * slope_se, slope_estimate),
    tol = 1e-10
  )$root,
  upper = uniroot(
    profile_equation,
    c(slope_estimate, slope_estimate + 10 * slope_se),
    tol = 1e-10
  )$root
)
software_profile_link <- suppressMessages(confint(
  fit,
  parm = "verb_typeresult"
))

stopifnot(
  max(abs(direct_profile_link - software_profile_link)) < 1e-3,
  max(abs(vapply(
    direct_profile_link,
    profile_equation,
    numeric(1L)
  ))) < 1e-6
)

data.frame(
  scale = c("log odds", "odds ratio"),
  lower = c(direct_profile_link[[1L]], exp(direct_profile_link[[1L]])),
  upper = c(direct_profile_link[[2L]], exp(direct_profile_link[[2L]]))
)
```

The intervals shown use the GLM's row independence assumption so that we can work through the calculation. The source paper obtains its inferential result from a model that also represents repeated participants and sentence materials. The observed contrast likewise supplies no evidence that verb type causes a completion choice.

## Recap, check, and scope

1. Why are probability-scale interval widths asymmetric? The symmetric interval was constructed on the logit scale and then transformed nonlinearly.
2. What does the fit establish? It describes a sample contrast under a Bernoulli model that treats rows as independent. It does not establish causality or participant independent uncertainty.

[Logistic regression with multiple predictors](logistic-regression-with-multiple-predictors.qmd) asks whether this contrast changes across contentfulness classes; [generalized linear mixed models](generalized-linear-mixed-models.qmd) later represent repeated units.
